data.title: Real income growth slows, non-PMET unemployment up: MOM sees signs of Singapore’s labour market moderating
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The Republic’s labour market “signs of moderation” in 2026, as real income grew at a slower pace and unemployment rose among non-PMETs (professionals, managers, executives and technicians).

Job mobility also fell, the Labour Force in Singapore Advance Release published on Friday (Nov 27) showed. The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) added: “Forward-looking indicators suggest that firms remained cautious about expanding headcount and raising wages.”

Still, the ministry called the labour market “resilient”. It remains tight, with high permanent employment (of 91 per cent among employed residents), and overqualification trending down slightly, pointed out Ang Boon Heng, director of its manpower research and statistics department.

Singapore’s overqualification rate declined to 18.7 per cent in 2026, from 19.4 per cent before, with a large majority of overqualified workers voluntarily taking roles below their qualification level.

“Overall, we continued to see a workforce characterised by relatively stable employment and an increasing share in higher-skilled roles,” the MOM said.

Moderating real income growth

Real incomes have continued to rise, while overall unemployment and time-related unemployment remain low, Ang highlighted.

The nominal median gross monthly income of full-time employed residents grew to S$6,021 in 2026, from S$5,775 in the year before. This marked the first time the indicator crossed the S$6,000 mark, and represents a record high, said Ang.

At the 20th percentile, nominal income grew to S$3,270, from S$3,164 before.

However, the pace of growth was slower in 2026 than in 2025 both in nominal terms and when inflation was taken into account. Real income growth at the median moderated from 4.1 per cent to 2.2 per cent, while growth at the 20th percentile eased from 3.6 per cent to 1.3 per cent.

“The moderation partly reflected more cautious wage increases by firms and higher inflation,” MOM said, adding that real income growth at the 20th percentile was higher than at the median over the recent five- and ten-year periods.

More churn for non-PMETs

Resident unemployment rates stayed low overall, with the unemployment rate of PMETs holding broadly steady at 2.7 per cent in 2026, compared with 2.8 per cent in the year before.

But the unemployment rate of non-PMETs grew from 2.8 per cent in 2025 to 3.5 per cent in 2026. This increase – to levels seen in 2023 and 2024 – was largely driven by older workers, noted Ang.

The non-PMET workforce, which includes roles such as service staff and cleaners, tends to see more churn, he said.

“We don’t see that this increase in unemployment rate among non-PMETs has translated to prolonged or sustained difficulties in securing employment.”

Long-term unemployment rates edged up to 0.7 per cent for both PMETs (from 0.6 per cent in 2025) and non-PMETs (from 0.5 per cent).

“These are close to historical averages, although the PMET rate was at the higher end of the range, reflecting softer hiring in outward-oriented sectors,” MOM said.

The number of discouraged workers, who do not seek work because they believe their job search would be unsuccessful, remained low at 7,100, or 0.3 per cent of the resident labour force – the same proportion as in the two years prior.

Time-related under-employment, which measures the share of part-time workers who are willing and able to take on more work, fell to 1.7 per cent, from 1.9 per cent in the year before.

Fewer switches, higher pay

Job mobility also slipped in 2026, with fewer residents changing jobs amid lower turnover and softer hiring.

The proportion of employed residents who changed jobs in the previous year declined to 5.7 per cent in 2026, from 6.2 per cent in 2025 – extending a gradual downtrend from a job-switching peak in 2022.

Of these job switches, 94.4 per cent were voluntary, rather than due to retrenchments.

Some 65.6 per cent of resident job switchers aged 25 to 64 experienced increases to their real income after changing jobs – with more than half (57.3 per cent) posting gains of at least 5 per cent.

Pay outcomes were better for voluntary job switchers – 67 per cent reported higher income in their new role, compared with 57.5 per cent for involuntary job switchers.

The MOM found that job switchers whose real income increased were more commonly degree holders and PMETs, as they were more likely to work in sectors with above-average productivity, such as financial and insurance services or infocommunications.

Older population, lower participation

Singapore’s resident labour force participation rate (LFPR) continued to ease in 2026, extending a decline that has been recorded since 2021. The trend mainly reflected Singapore’s population ageing and retiring, rather than weaker economic conditions, MOM said. 

The LFPR for residents aged 15 and over dipped to 67.8 per cent in 2026, from 67.9 per cent in 2025, despite stable or slightly higher participation rates for residents in the prime working age range of 25 to 54 years and for seniors.

As a super-aged society, the share of residents aged 65 and over among the working age population continued to grow, and this group generally has lower participation rates than younger age groups, MOM said.

Still, Singapore’s overall LFPR remained among the highest compared with Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development countries – a fact that Ang believes may be because other countries are facing similar challenges, as well as because Singapore has been implementing measures to encourage hiring and labour force retention of senior workers.

Released annually, the Labour Force in Singapore Advance Release looks at structural indicators in the job market, rather than quarter-on-quarter movements.

data.title: Why a professional baseline for HR is a reasonable expectation
data.description:
IF THE pace of change feels faster, it is because it is. New artificial intelligence systems are arriving at speed and organisations are moving them from experiments into everyday workflows.

In conversations with business and human resources (HR) leaders, I hear the same questions: Which tasks should be automated? How should decisions be made? And how must operating models evolve to ensure that technology improves performance without leaving people behind?

For workers, these are not abstract questions. Familiar tasks may disappear while new ones emerge. Skills built over many years may no longer be enough.

The result is a mixture of anticipation and anxiety, particularly when change affects a person’s livelihood, career prospects and sense of what lies ahead.

Technology is only one part of this transformation. Singapore is also facing rapid population ageing.

In 2026, citizens aged 65 and above made up 21.4 per cent of Singapore’s citizen population, placing the country above the threshold commonly used to define a super-aged society.

As more people remain in the workforce for longer, employers will need to redesign jobs, provide flexible work arrangements and build workplaces where different generations can contribute and learn from one another.

The regulatory landscape is also evolving. Parliament has passed the Workplace Fairness Act and the accompanying dispute-resolution legislation, both of which are scheduled to take effect at the end of 2027.

Employers will need stronger systems for fair employment decisions, grievance handling and documentation. What was once guided mainly by tripartite norms will increasingly carry statutory obligations and consequences.

Taken together, these shifts raise a straightforward question: What should employers and workers be able to expect from the professionals who advise on decisions that carry legal risk and can alter working lives?

This question lies at the heart of the recent report by the Tripartite Workgroup on Human Capital Capability Development, which sets out five recommendations to strengthen Singapore’s human capital capabilities.

One proposal has attracted particular attention: from Jul 1, 2028, organisations with more than 200 employees will need at least one HR professional certified at the Institute for Human Resource Practitioners (IHRP) Certified Professional level or higher.

Recognised equivalent accreditations may also qualify, subject to applicable bridging requirements.

These concerns are understandable. A certificate cannot capture everything that makes a good HR professional. It cannot fully measure empathy, courage or judgment, nor predict how someone will respond when an employee’s role is at risk or a business faces a painful restructuring.

Neither should experienced practitioners without certification be dismissed as incapable; many have built deep expertise over decades.

However, the limits of certification are not an argument against a professional baseline.

When someone advises on employment rights, workplace fairness, grievances or restructuring, employers and workers should have confidence that the individual has demonstrated a recognised foundation of HR knowledge, ethics and professional judgment.

A baseline should also not be mistaken for a one-off examination that divides the capable from the incapable. Professional certification should be a continuing commitment: a standard that evolves with business, technology, regulation and workforce expectations.

IHRP’s framework is anchored in its Body of Competencies, which was first introduced in 2016 and subsequently refreshed in 2020 and 2024 through engagement with business and HR leaders, tripartite partners and the wider ecosystem.

Some have pointed out that experience matters more. Indeed, experience remains indispensable. It deepens perspective and helps practitioners recognise patterns that no textbook can teach.

Yet, experience can also harden into familiar assumptions. Pairing it with an evolving professional standard gives practitioners reason to test what they think they know, update their knowledge and keep their judgment current.

There is a broader point here about the standing of HR I hope can be further debated. When people think of the professions on which society depends, they often cite medicine, law, accountancy and engineering.

HR should be part of this conversation too. HR practitioners apply specialised knowledge, exercise professional judgment, uphold ethical standards and advise on decisions with serious consequences for individuals and organisations.

Professional recognition should reflect this level of responsibility. This requirement is an important step towards positioning HR alongside other recognised professions – a profession that our community can be proud of.

IHRP, for its part, has work to do. Certification must remain rigorous, accessible and relevant. The standards must keep pace with generative AI, flexible work, new workforce models and the responsible use of people data.

Recertification must reflect genuine professional development rather than become a passive pay-to-maintain exercise. Together with learning and ecosystem partners, we must give practitioners practical ways to learn, find mentors, exchange experience and support one another.

Ultimately, the measure of professionalisation will not be the number of certificates issued. It will be whether employment practices become fairer, workforce planning improves, difficult decisions are handled more responsibly and trust in HR grows.

A professional baseline cannot guarantee these outcomes. However, at a time when employers face increasingly complex and consequential decisions, it is a reasonable place to start.

The writer is chief executive officer of the IHRP

data.title: HSBC reorganises India support roles, impacting hundreds of jobs
data.description:
HSBC is consolidating some support functions in India as the Asia-focused lender steps up efforts to rein in costs and accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence. 

The bank recently told employees in India that it was centralising finance functions across cities including Chennai, Gurugram and Bangalore and will no longer be housing those roles in other hubs, including Hyderabad and Pune, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested not to be named because the information is private.

The changes are confined to finance roles within HSBC’s so-called global capability centres in India, and employees expect the move to affect several hundred roles, according to the people.

HSBC staff will be given the option and support to relocate, but the bank won’t provide further cash incentives for them to move, the people added.

HSBC has been weighing deep job cuts over the coming years as chief executive officer Georges Elhedery deploys AI to shrink its middle and back offices.

Non-client facing roles in global service centres are among those expected to be most impacted, people familiar have said previously. The changes could ultimately impact around 20,000 roles — or about 10 per cent of its total workforce.

“As we simplify the bank, our focus remains on ensuring we have the right roles in the right locations to support the best customer outcomes,” an HSBC spokesperson said in a statement, referring to the roles in India.

“We are taking the best of our people experience and combining this with emerging technologies to deliver outcomes that are better, faster, and safer for our clients.”

India has emerged as a key market for HSBC, alongside other major banks. HSBC describes itself as the largest foreign lender in the country and generated US$1.9 billion of pretax profit in the region in 2025.

It had about 47,000 employees in India at the end of last year. About 42,500 employees work in the global capability centers in India, including on technology, according to estimates from a person familiar with the matter.

Other banks have also been reshaping their Indian hubs, which have grown so large that Goldman Sachs Group and JPMorgan now employ more people in India than anywhere else outside the US.

They are using AI to automate work such as checking loan documents, reconciling accounts and writing basic code, the same tasks that once gave fresh graduates their first jobs at those centres. 

Lenders globally are expecting AI to lead to fewer roles in the future. Standard Chartered plans to cut close to 8,000 support roles over four years, while JPMorgan Chase & Co. CEO Jamie Dimon has said the technology will eliminate jobs broadly across industries.

Banks are trimming junior analyst classes by as much as two-thirds, Debasish Patnaik, a senior partner at McKinsey & Co., said in June.

At HSBC, Elhedery has accelerated an overhaul of Europe’s largest bank through asset sales and operational simplification. 

In August, the lender said it expects its global restructuring effort to yield US$2 billion in cost savings, up from an earlier target of US$1.5 billion. The banker has made streamlining HSBC a central principle, saying earlier this year that he had been “ruthless about killing complexity” at the lender. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Human oversight in AI should be measured, not assumed
data.description:
RECENT reports in The Business Times have highlighted that clear permissions, audit trails, well-governed data and human sign-off on consequential decisions are key safeguards for financial institutions deploying artificial intelligence agents.

But keeping a human in the loop is not, by itself, a sufficient control. The more useful question is what risk that human checkpoint is meant to reduce, and whether it actually does so.

At the recent Global Finance & Technology Network session on AI innovation and governance, I asked a senior leader at a global bank whether an agent’s mandate could change in real time as conditions changed. The response was candid. It was a difficult question requiring further analysis.

That matters because human review can become a significant constraint as agentic workflows scale. McKinsey found that for a banking customer-service agent, human oversight accounted for 70 to 75 per cent of variable run costs, compared with 20 to 25 per cent for token costs.

The figures will differ across workflows, but they expose an important trade-off. Applying human approval too broadly can undermine the efficiency automation is meant to create.

Oversight should therefore follow the risk. A suspected fraud case, rejected loan, or large transfer to a new counterparty may warrant human judgment.

An agent assembling documents or updating an internal workflow within tightly defined permissions may not. The relevant factors include customer impact, value at risk, reversibility and uncertainty.

That principle is consistent with the AI risk-management guidelines from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), which urge financial institutions to apply controls proportionately according to their risk exposure and the scale and nature of their AI use.

MAS’ Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime Framework complements that direction with more granular guidance on how agent actions can be authorised, recorded and escalated for human review.

Banks should apply the same discipline to human oversight.

There is no single formula for assessing whether a checkpoint works. The industry will need evidence on where intervention catches material problems, changes proposed actions or adds delay without reducing risk.

A checkpoint may remain necessary for audit or accountability, even if interventions are rare.

The bank should be able to explain what risk it controls.

Crucially, this rule book cannot remain static. Agents act at machine speed, while the policies, mandates and controls governing them still change at human speed.

As agents take on new tasks, banks will need to revisit whether their escalation points still match the risks.

The goal is not maximum autonomy or maximum human involvement; it is to put human judgment where it changes the outcome. Every escalation should have a clear purpose.

Wei You Pan Field chief technology officer, MongoDB

data.title: Stocks to watch: Kimly, AP Oil, Heptamax
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 26):

Kimly : The coffee shop operator reported a 30.8 per cent fall in net profit to S$12.8 million for its second half ended Sep 30, from S$18.5 million a year earlier. Revenue came in 1 per cent lower at S$161.1 million, from S$162.8 million previously. Kimly proposed a final dividend of S$0.01 a share for H2, bringing the total FY2026 dividend to S$0.02 a share. Shares of Kimly ended flat at S$0.365 on Wednesday, before the news.

AP Oil : The CEO of the petroleum products company, Ho Chee Hon, was sentenced to six months jail and a fine of S$25,000 for drink-driving on Wednesday. Accordingly, he will be away on a leave of absence for a period of six months from Dec 1. The company said that the charges are personal in nature and unrelated to its business or operations. Its board added that Ho remains suitable to continue in his role as CEO. Shares of AP Oil ended flat at S$0.126 on Wednesday, before the update.

Heptamax : The industrial solutions company, which is proposing to buy a data centre company for S$500 million in a reverse takeover, has been queried by the Singapore Exchange Regulation over the deal. Among other things, the regulator asked how the valuation for the target company Racks Central was arrived at. It also asked Heptamax to give details of the beneficial owners of the vendor. The company replied that the price was arrived at on a willing-buyer, willing-seller basis, taking into account Racks Central’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation for FY2025, among other things. Heptamax ended flat at S$0.131 on Wednesday.

data.title: Asia has less to fear from the AI correction than you might think
data.description:
IN THE semiconductor manufacturing hubs of Taiwan and South Korea, financial regulators are worried about the mounting risks of the artificial-intelligence boom.

On Nov 19, Taiwan’s Financial Supervisory Commission tightened curbs on short selling to help stabilise the stock market, after its benchmark index suffered its sharpest weekly decline since 1991.

Meanwhile, South Korean policymakers are considering activating a 10.7 trillion won (US$8 billion) stock market stabilisation fund. The Kospi has lost a staggering 48 per cent since hitting a record high on Jun 22.

It is hard to overstate the impact of the AI infrastructure build-out on Asia’s economies. In 2024, seven of the top 10 exporters of AI-enabling goods were in Asia, including Singapore and Malaysia, the only South-east Asian economies with front-end chip manufacturing capabilities.

The Asia-Pacific’s share of global data centre capacity is expected to exceed 40 per cent by 2030. Within the region, South-east Asia accounts for the largest proportion of capacity under construction, led by Malaysia and Thailand.

Gone are the days when the technology-heavy US stock market had the highest AI concentration risk.

In the MSCI Asia Pacific ex-Japan index, the information technology and communication services sectors have a combined 46 per cent weighting.

Taiwan and South Korea alone account for nearly 50 per cent of the entire emerging market equity index.

Asia under scrutiny

The dramatic unravelling of the AI trade across global markets since early October has put Asia under intense scrutiny. A succession of shocks has fanned fears over the financing, regulation and geopolitics of the AI build-out.

The plunge in US tech shares, the angst over the scale of AI-related debt issuance, and the threat of a clampdown on US data centre construction following the decisive victory of the Democrats in the midterm elections have undermined confidence in the AI narrative.

Moreover, the spying scandal engulfing Nvidia has ensnared South-east Asia, as US authorities scrutinise alleged chip diversion to China through the region.

New rules unveiled by the US Commerce Department seek to close a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s cutting-edge AI chips remotely by renting computing power from South-east Asian data centres and cloud providers.

The Institute for Progress, a US think tank, estimates remote access will account for nearly one-third of China’s AI chip stock by the end of next year, with South-east Asia expected to comprise 72 per cent of China’s overseas AI compute.

HSBC says “efforts to restrict mainland China’s access to advanced technology could become a broader investment and demand shock for (South-east Asia).”

Not so fast. While Asia is acutely vulnerable to a slowdown in the AI investment cycle, the region foreshadowed the financial and regulatory risks of the boom, helping blunt the impact of the recent turmoil in the US tech sector.

South Korea’s equity market was the canary in the coal mine for the AI trade. Foreign funds had already dumped US$130 billion of the country’s stocks in 2026 prior to the sell-off in the US, contributing to steep declines in Asian tech shares over the summer. This has made the region’s equity markets look increasingly undervalued, especially given the enduring strength of corporate earnings.

In a sign of the degree to which AI demand remains exceptionally buoyant, Goldman Sachs expects profit growth for the Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index in 2027 to reach 26 per cent, driven by the tech hardware and chip sectors in South Korea and Taiwan.

Regulatory realities

Furthermore, fears about the impact of tougher regulatory scrutiny of the AI build-out on South-east Asia’s economies are overdone.

While the new US-export licensing rules will test regional operators in the near term, the region has benefited from restrictions on data centre development designed to ensure the boom does not turn to bust.

Singapore’s full-blown moratorium on new construction in 2019 to 2022 was a catalyst for the surge in investment in the Malaysian state of Johor, currently the largest data centre market in the Asia-Pacific when combining operational and planned capacity.

It was also the precursor to the imposition of regulations across South-east Asia designed to balance sustainability requirements with digital infrastructure needs, creating a more resilient data centre market. The region’s neutrality, moreover, cuts both ways.

While many anchor tenants of data centres in Malaysia and Thailand are Chinese, a large portion is American. This “could divert more incremental demand towards (Malaysia) if (data centre) regulations tighten in the US”, notes Citigroup.

Lastly, it is important to put the threats to the AI build-out into perspective.

First, non-AI workloads – traditional compute and cloud services – accounted for nearly half of global data centre demand in 2025, said McKinsey.

In Asia, where digital infrastructure is at an earlier stage of the growth cycle, the share was much higher. Strong domestic and regional demand provide a buffer against a slowdown in the AI capital expenditure cycle.

Second, anti-data centre politicians’ bark is worse than their bite. In the US, Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic governor-elect of Texas – which accounts for one quarter of the nation’s planned data centre capacity – said construction of facilities with permits will be allowed to proceed.

In fact, stricter rules for approving new data centres should help ease concern over the financing of the AI boom. A slower, more expensive and selective build-out will increase the value of existing AI data centres, as the mismatch between strong demand and supply constraints intensifies.

Third, portfolio diversification in the age of AI is easier said than done, particularly in Asia.

While India is touted as the “anti-AI trade” because of its limited exposure to tech hardware, many fund managers see this as a liability and believe AI capital expenditure and monetisation will continue to drive returns in Asian equity markets.

The AI narrative remains compelling.

That Nvidia, under pressure from US President Donald Trump, reinstated the scandal-tainted Jensen Huang as its CEO shows that the build-out has a strong political backstop – one that limits how far lawmakers can let the AI trade unwind without hurting tens of trillions of dollars in American retirement savings.

Asia’s crucial role in the AI supply chain makes it a key gauge of investor sentiment. More volatility is inevitable. All the more reason not to lose sight of the powerful drivers of the region’s digital infrastructure boom.

The writer is an independent adviser and columnist

data.title: Asean must counter economic nationalism with deeper integration, wider partnerships: DPM Gan
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Asean must counter rising economic nationalism with deeper integration and wider partnerships, in a world where governments are placing more emphasis on self-reliance and control over critical industries, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong on Nov 27.

“Raising barriers among ourselves would narrow the opportunities available to each of us,” he said. A more integrated Asean would strengthen its value as a partner, while broader tie-ups open up more opportunities for the region.

Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), was delivering a keynote speech at SPH Media’s Asia Future Summit 2026, jointly presented by The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

The annual event gathered policymakers, business leaders and industry experts, with OCBC as the presenting sponsor, Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

In his speech, Gan identified three factors that make integration and partnerships especially important: artificial intelligence, geopolitical shocks and geo-economic contestation. “Each can strengthen the impulse to turn inward. Yet each also makes cooperation more crucial,” he said.

His remarks followed the United States’ announcements of fresh tariffs and chip export restrictions over the past two weeks, moves which affected many in South-east Asia as the region finds itself in the crosshairs of sharpening rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

“Geo-economic competition is reshaping the networks through which we trade, invest and access technology,” Gan said, with governments paying closer attention to dependencies and control over critical capabilities.

“Asean countries cannot determine how major powers manage their differences,” he added. “But we can maintain relationships across these divides and remain a bridge for trade, investment and cooperation.”

Doing so would require that Asean earn and sustain its partners’ confidence in the grouping’s integrity, institutional reliability and business environment by issuing clear and predictable rules, upholding its laws and commitments, and taking firm action against wrongdoing, he said.

“As scrutiny of international trade and investment intensifies, maintaining these standards becomes even more important,” he added.

ASEAN will mark its 60th anniversary in 2027, with Singapore pushing for deeper integration and wider partnerships as it takes on Asean’s rotating chairmanship at a time of heightened geopolitical contestation.

Both the US and China would continue to be key economic partners for Asean, Gan said, with their businesses, technologies and markets important to the region’s growth.

Both countries are among the region’s largest trading partners and sources of foreign direct investment.

In tandem, the grouping is strengthening tie-ups with other partners that would expand the region’s economic options and reduce its exposure to disruptions, Gan said.

These include negotiations to upgrade Asean’s trade agreements with South Korea and Canada, moves to expand and enhance the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and growing links with other regional groupings such as the European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council.

Asean is also strengthening integration within the grouping, with Gan highlighting recent efforts that would help firms better tap suppliers and customers within the region.

A recently upgraded Asean Trade in Goods Agreement, set to be rolled out in end-2026, will help businesses reduce costs through streamlined procedures and more transparent rules, he said, while a customs-related mutual recognition arrangement would give trusted traders faster clearances and priority treatment in participating countries.

And a regional Digital Economy Framework Agreement signed earlier in the month would make cross-border transactions, payments and access to digital services easier, he added.

These would make Asean more valuable as a place to produce and market to serve, and form a stronger regional base enabling the grouping to “engage the world with greater confidence”, Gan said. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: AI here to stay despite tech bifurcation: OCBC chief Tan Teck Long
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Falling artificial intelligence costs are continuously lowering the hurdle for corporates to boost productivity, and will lead to readier and wider use of AI in the years ahead, OCBC group CEO Tan Teck Long said on Friday (Nov 27).

Speaking at the Asia Future Summit 2026, amid a global tech rout fuelled by concerns over AI investment, Tan said AI is here to stay. “Despite the current worries about AI-related stocks, AI is here to stay given increased adoption, improved AI model capability and declining cost of AI.”

The OCBC chief was delivering the opening address at the annual thought leadership conference, which returned for its fifth edition this year.

For the first time, it was jointly presented by SPH Media’s key news titles: The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

OCBC is the presenting sponsor, with Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

In his opening remarks, he noted Asia’s role in shaping supply chains and how AI is used.

While AI adoption may become more widespread, the technology landscape supporting that adoption could become more fragmented.

The future is likely to see bifurcation in technology standards, differentiated access to technology and possibly AI models, he said.

The way he sees it, the optimal path forward – balancing cost and security considerations – appears to be a mix of open and closed-source models.

Open-source ones, which many Chinese AI models are, allow users to bring them on premise and customise them to their needs, he said.

Closed-source ones, which are more common among American AI models, may be fast to set up, but are a black box to users, he continued.

But Tan maintained that technological bifurcation does not mean complete supply chain separation. “Even as technology controls tighten, the underlying supply chain remains deeply connected.”

He added that, despite trade tariff disruptions, intra-Asia trade remains on the rise and accounts for more than half of the region’s total trade. Likewise, foreign direct investment into Asean continues to grow, anchored by supply chain diversification and AI-driven investments.

Regional trade agreements and collaboration will be key to sustaining this growth momentum, he said.

Digital-green convergence

AI can also be leveraged to promote green energy, noted Tan.

“When OCBC finances data centres, we note that tech companies are increasingly demanding clean energy to meet sustainability goals,” he said. “Data centres are very power hungry and those supporting AI even more so.”

Whether existing power grids can support all the demand remains to be seen.

But, in the data centre world, it is increasingly about bringing your own power, and such demand can help to spur the development of green energy, he said.

Tan raised the example of how OCBC provides green financing for a Singapore data centre pioneering a hydrogen energy proof-of-concept, as well as for data centres using solar energy.

Heightened cyber threats

But, as AI adoption grows, so do the risks of exposure to heightened cyber threats and scams, he contended.

He pointed to investment scam losses in Singapore, which totalled S$170 million in the first half of the year and accounted for some 40 per cent of total scam losses. Such scams are the costliest category by dollar amount, he noted.

OCBC is helping to lead the banking industry’s fight against scams, said the bank chief.

Collective efforts have made a difference, as total scam losses fell 18 per cent in the first half of the year while investment scams declined 5 per cent, he pointed out.
